title: Milk and water
hookLine: Anuruddha and his friends live blended like milk and water

lines: THE QUIET WAR IN A SHARED KITCHEN.
THREE MONKS IN A SAL-TREE WOOD.
cards: Every shared kitchen has the same quiet war. Who finishes the milk and doesn't buy more. Who leaves the pan soaking for three days.

Who takes the trash out, every single time, and has started keeping score. Three monks once lived together in a sal-tree wood called Gosinga. When the Buddha came to visit, he asked how they were getting along.

teach.h: THE PARK KEEPER TRIES TO TURN HIM AWAY
teach.b: In the thirty-first discourse of the Middle-Length Sayings, the three are Anuruddha, Nandiya and Kimbila.
When the Buddha arrives, the park keeper, not knowing who he is, tries to turn him away so as not to disturb the monks. Anuruddha hears, and comes running. Are you living in harmony? the Buddha asks.
Yes, says Anuruddha: we live without quarreling, blending like milk and water, looking at each other with kind eyes. How? I think, how fortunate I am to live with companions like these.

teach.h: KINDNESS IN DEED, WORD AND THOUGHT
teach.b: I treat them with kindness in deed, word and thought, openly and in private. And I think, why don't I set aside what I want, and do what they want? So I do.
We are different in body, he says, but one in mind. Then he describes the kitchen. Whoever comes back first from the alms round sets out the seats and the water.
Whoever comes back last eats what's left or throws it out, and puts everything away.

teach.h: WHOEVER SEES THE JAR EMPTY FILLS IT
teach.b: Whoever sees the water jar empty fills it. If it's too heavy, he waves a hand for help, and the two of them carry it together, without breaking the silence.
And every fifth night they sit up together, talking about the teaching. Milk and water mix so completely you can't pour them apart again.

teach.h: THIS WEEK: FROM AN ANTHILL TO A JAR
teach.b: In Anuruddha's telling, that blend is built from small things: a filled jar, a tidied seat, nobody keeping score.
And the week looks back: an anthill dug carefully, relay chariots, the bait, ariyapariyesana, a footprint, the heartwood, and now the whole path in a water jar carried by two.

how: Buddhist monasteries still share chores in much the way MN 31 describes, and the phrase 'like milk and water' is often used by Buddhist teachers to describe the ideal of a harmonious community, lay or monastic.

o: in harmony, blended like milk and water
of one family, born to the same parents
following one strict rule of silence

games.q: life in the Gosinga wood — tap the pairs.
p: eats what's left and tidies up
the water jar is too heavy
wave a hand, carry it together

s: the park keeper welcomed the Buddha in
not knowing who he was, he tried to turn him away so the monks wouldn't be disturbed.
Anuruddha says they are different in body but one in mind
he sets aside what he wants and does what his companions want.
the monks talked while carrying the water jar
the one who needed help waved a hand, and they carried it together without breaking the silence.

games.q: you're one of the three monks. you come back last from the alms round. there's leftover food and the seats are still out. what do you do?
o: leave it for whoever was first; they set it up.
eat what's left or throw it out, and put everything away.
games.why: in Anuruddha's description, whoever comes back last eats what's left or throws it out, and puts the seats and water away. nobody needs to be asked.

practice: Think of someone you share space with, a home, an office, a group chat, and try Anuruddha's thought just to see how it feels: how fortunate I am to live with this person. It may feel strange; let it.
Then picture one small thing you could do for them without being asked or mentioning it, the jar, the dishes, the trash, and breathe with that picture.

wordCard.voice: samagga. Lives blended so well they pour as one: kind in deed, word and thought, each setting aside what they want for the others.

orig.note: Pali samagga: in concord, united. after asking after their health and alms, the Buddha asks the three whether they live in concord.

carryVoice: Your line: nobody keeping score. Different in body, one in mind, as Anuruddha put it. A week, done.
